How to Report for 100+ Clients With One Semantic Model

Configuration-driven reporting: one semantic model, one metric catalog, and a few lines of configuration per audience

VAL YE
November 5, 202611 min read
Prefer us on Google

If you report to many audiences, you have probably built the same report more than once. Agencies build one report per client. Consultancies build one report per engagement. Internal analytics teams build one report per business unit, brand or market. Each copy begins as a reasonable response to a real difference, and each copy becomes one more place for a definition to live.

The standard answer is a metrics layer: define each metric once and make every dashboard read that definition. The design in this article contains one. A metrics layer assumes one organization, one vocabulary and one set of data. A hundred unrelated clients sharing one model is a different problem. Each of them calls the metrics by its own names, sends its own data and keeps its own calendar, and none of them may have the shared model changed on its behalf.

I designed a system for that case on the analytics team of an agency that bought podcast, radio, YouTube and other media for its clients. About ten analysts each carried between eight and twenty accounts, every account had its own report, and the only plan for growth was another analyst for every ten new clients. What replaced that was one data model, one metric catalog, one report template, and a short settings record per client. The same template ended up serving more than a hundred clients. This article builds the design up one complication at a time. Everything in it runs in a small companion repository with synthetic data and three fictional clients.

Learn this step by step with the interactive Data Engineer roadmap.

The fixed model

Start with the easy case: ten clients, all watching cost per acquisition (CPA), which is spend divided by conversions. Ten reports with ten CPA formulas work until the definition changes and one copy is missed.

The alternative is one table. Every client's data lands in it, with the same columns, at the same level of detail:

Three rows of the synthetic data in the companion repository. The empty cells are deliberate.

This is a fact table at the center of a dimensional model: one row per client, campaign, channel and day. That fixed level of detail is the grain. Everything that follows depends on it, and it is the first decision I would make in any new reporting system.

CPA is now defined exactly once:

sql 
sum(spend) / nullif(sum(conversions), 0)

The client is a filter. In the original system the report template's load script had a single where client = ... clause. Changing that one value switched every chart and every label to another client.

Same math, different names

The first complication arrives before the tenth client does. Clients agree on the math far more often than they agree on the words. One client's CPA is another client's CPO, cost per order. One client calls traffic sessions, and another calls it visits. One client calls revenue divided by spend ROAS, and another calls the same number ROI.

The reverse happens too. "Acquisition" meant a completed order for one client, a checkout started for another, and a site visit for a third. "ROI" meant revenue over spend for one client and profit over spend for another. An analyst covering a colleague's account could apply the wrong definition without knowing it.

If the name lives inside the formula, every renaming becomes a new metric and the copies drift apart. So I separated the two. The definition lives once, in the catalog. The name lives in the client's settings. At onboarding, every KPI gets two questions: how do you calculate it, and what do you call it? The first answer maps to an existing definition, or becomes a new one, once, for everyone. The second answer becomes a label:

yaml 
brewbox:  name: BrewBox Coffee Subscription  week_start: monday  conversion: Trial  kpi_types: [cpa]  sends: [spend, impressions, sessions, conversions]  labels: {sessions: Visits}

BrewBox's report says "Cost per Trial" and "Visits" over the same SQL every other client gets. Whatever a client's primary outcome is, trial, install or order, it lands in one generic conversions column, and the record supplies the word. The {conversion} placeholder in the catalog is filled from this record, which is how BrewBox gets Cost per Trial. A client that wants revenue over spend shown as "ROI" gets a label on roas. A client that means profit over spend gets a different definition, roi. Two clients can both see a column called ROI and get different math, as long as the catalog knows which is which. The reporting week is in the record too, because a weekly number on the wrong week is a wrong number. The sends line is the subject of a later section.

This is where the design parts ways with a plain metrics layer. A metrics layer gives a metric one name. This gives it one meaning and as many names as there are clients.

What if some clients watch different KPIs?

Client eleven is an online store. It watches return on ad spend. Building a second report would start the copies again.

So the report stops naming metrics. The template asks for "KPI 1" through "KPI N", and each client's settings decide what fills each slot. The catalog groups metrics into templates by goal: the CPA template is spend, conversions, CPA, sessions and conversion rate; the ROAS template is spend, revenue, ROAS, conversions and average order value.

A client picks one or more templates, and a small piece of code between the template and the database, the resolver, merges them in order and drops duplicates. The first version of this system picked one template per client and handled the few clients that wanted both by hand. Merging makes "both" an ordinary case.

Unused slots never appear as empty columns. In the BI tool, each KPI column carried a "show column if" condition that read the client's settings, so a client using three of ten slots saw three columns, not ten.

What if clients send different data?

This was the hardest problem in practice and the one I see discussed least.

A third party does not own its clients' data. Spend and impressions come from the buyer's own booking records, so every client has them; they are listed under sends anyway, so the availability check has one rule. Performance data comes from the client, and the client decides what to send. One client sends orders and nothing else. Another sends orders, sessions and revenue. An app client has installs but no website sessions at all.

The CPA template includes conversion rate, which is conversions divided by sessions. What should it show for the client with no sessions? Zero would be wrong, because zero means measured and found to be zero. An error message has no place on a client-facing report. A separate template for every combination of data is where the old approach was heading.

Two declarations fix it. Every metric declares what it is made of:

yaml 
# semantic/metrics.yaml (abridged: display format and direction omitted)base:  spend:       {column: spend}  sessions:    {column: sessions}  conversions: {column: conversions}  revenue:     {column: revenue}ratio:  cpa:  {label: "Cost per {conversion}", num: spend,       den: conversions}  cvr:  {label: "Conversion rate",       num: conversions, den: sessions}  roas: {label: "ROAS",                  num: revenue,     den: spend}  aov:  {label: "Average order value",   num: revenue,     den: conversions}

Every client declares what it sends; that is the sends line in BrewBox's record. The resolver checks each wanted metric against that list. Supported metrics take a slot. The rest are left off, and the report says why:

markdown 
Not shown- Sessions: needs sessions, which this client does not send.- Conversion rate: needs sessions, which this client does not send.

When a client asks why conversion rate is missing, the answer is on the page, and it points at the data rather than at the analyst. It also turns a complaint into a request: send sessions, and conversion rate appears, with no new report and no code change.

The same declaration standardizes intake. Once the model says what it needs, a new client can be told exactly what shape to send.

The ratio trap

The fact table has no CPA column, no ROAS column and no conversion rate column. That is the one rule I would keep if I had to throw everything else away: store the parts, never the ratio.

Average the daily CPAs and you get $60. Divide total spend by total conversions and you get $33.33, which is the campaign's actual CPA. The average weights a 10-conversion day the same as a 50-conversion day. Every ratio is therefore computed as sum(numerator) / sum(denominator) after grouping, at whatever level the report asks for. Day, week, channel or whole quarter, the definition is the same and the number is right. The whole family of "why doesn't the weekly number match the daily numbers" questions goes away. In the original system these ratios were expressions in the dashboard. The dataset held only raw measures.

What if the data arrives at a different grain?

Everything so far assumes one row per client, campaign, channel and day, and the design worked because nearly every source fit that grain. When a source does not, the same approach applies with one more table. The usual case is a radio vendor that sends weekly totals. The weekly source gets its own fact table on the same dimensions, reports roll the daily table up to weeks and combine the two at the coarser grain, and the report says it goes no finer than a week.

Two rules keep this honest. A weekly total is never spread across days, because that invents detail nobody measured. And a weekly source whose weeks do not start on the client's week start fails the build, because no query can realign those totals without guessing. Measures that do not add, unique reach above all, sit outside the pattern entirely and must be computed from source at the level requested.

Where it fits

This fits any team that produces the same kind of report for many audiences that each want their own numbers in it, as long as the audiences share a grain and a core set of measures and differ mainly in vocabulary, KPI selection, data availability and calendar. Keep N small; an audience that needs something truly custom should get a custom page of its own. And treat configuration as a product: once a record changes a client's numbers, it needs validation, an owner and a history.

What it did in production

Building a client's dashboard became a configuration change, and build time fell by roughly 70%, from hours to minutes. Weekly reporting work fell by about a third. The same template served more than a hundred clients.

Two effects mattered as much as the time saved. Definitions stopped drifting, and nearly any analyst could pick up nearly any account, because everything account-specific was written down in the settings record. And because the record was a table, it joined to the performance data. Questions that used to depend on memory, such as which clients in an industry tracked orders and how quickly their campaigns saturated, became a filter on the settings followed by one query.

What I would change today

Keep configuration in version control. The original settings lived in the CRM, where the account information already was, and analysts edited them there. A record that changes a client's numbers deserves a diff, a review, and a check against the data it describes. The repository warns when a record and the data disagree about what a client sends.

Declare inputs from the start. The first version already hid unused slots, but deciding which KPIs a client's data could support was still a judgment made at setup. Declaring each metric's inputs turns that judgment into a rule, and the "Not shown" list says why.

Use a mature semantic layer at scale. Defining metrics once and resolving them per context is now a product category. A large team starting fresh should start there. A small team still gets most of the benefit from one fact table, one metric file and one record per client. Either way, the hard parts are the same: decide the grain, declare what each metric is made of, and be explicit about what each audience actually sends.

Conclusion

The design scaled because it separated what every client shares, which belongs in one model and one catalog, from what makes each client different, which belongs in a small, explicit record. Start with the grain. Store the parts and compute the ratios. Make each audience's differences a few lines of configuration. Then onboarding the next client means writing a record.

Try it yourself

The companion repository, config-driven-reporting, has a synthetic data generator, the shared model, the metric catalog, the KPI templates, settings for three fictional clients and one report template:

bash 
pip install -r requirements.txtmake

BrewBox tracks CPA on a Monday week and calls its sessions visits. PulseFit tracks CPA, has no session data, and has a radio source that only arrives weekly. Juniper tracks ROAS and CPA together under its own names. Add a fourth client to config/clients.yaml and the same template produces its report.

summary: 本文介绍了一套可扩展的报告系统，用统一的语义模型取代面向各个客户的多份专属报告。系统的核心包括一张粒度固定、存储可加性度量的事实表；一个集中式指标目录，用于统一定义计算逻辑；以及按客户维护的配置记录，用于指定名称、KPI 选择和数据可用性。主要创新包括将指标定义与标签分离、通过解析器根据客户设置动态组合报告，以及明确声明指标所需的输入，以妥善处理数据缺失。该系统将构建时间缩短了 70%，消除了指标定义偏差，并让任何分析师都能负责任何客户账户。作者建议对配置进行版本控制，并在大规模实施时使用成熟的语义层工具。

mainPoints.point: 所有客户共用一个粒度固定的维度模型，客户专属差异通过配置处理，而不是复制报表。
mainPoints.explanation: 事实表按日存储跨客户、营销活动和渠道的原始可加性度量。各客户在命名、KPI 选择和日历方面的差异通过外部配置记录管理，避免定义偏差，并使分析师能够相互接替工作。

mainPoints.point: 指标定义集中存放在目录中，而客户专属标签和 KPI 选择则通过配置驱动的解析器动态确定。
mainPoints.explanation: 每个指标只有一个标准定义（例如，CPA = 总支出 / 总转化次数），但可以针对不同客户使用不同名称。解析器根据客户设置选择合适的指标，通过列出「不显示」的原因来处理数据缺失，并且无需更改代码即可组合报告。

mainPoints.point: 比率根据已存储的组成数据计算，而非使用预先计算的列，以确保跨时间周期和维度汇总时结果正确。
mainPoints.explanation: 系统只存储原始度量（支出、转化次数、收入），并在查询时按总分子 / 总分母计算 CPA 等比率。这样可以避免对每日比率进行错误平均，并确保每周数值与每日汇总结果一致。

mainPoints.point: 明确声明每项指标所需的输入，可妥善处理不同客户的数据可用性差异。
mainPoints.explanation: 每个指标都会声明其所需输入（例如，转化率需要会话数）。解析器会检查客户的数据可用性，并排除不受支持的指标，同时明确说明「不显示」的原因，从而将数据缺口转化为可执行的数据请求，而不是报错。

mainPoints.point: 该架构将配置视为一种产品，通过验证、责任归属和版本控制实现扩展。
mainPoints.explanation: 配置记录应纳入版本控制，并保留差异记录和审核流程。系统还可以根据指标目录中的输入要求制定标准化数据接入规范，从而快速引入新客户。
